purpose: Sargramostim helps your body make more white blood cells, which are the cells that fight infection. It is used after chemotherapy, bone marrow transplants, or other treatments that lower your white blood cell count. It can also help speed up recovery of your immune system so you are less likely to get serious infections.
how_it_works: Your bone marrow is like a factory that makes blood cells. Sargramostim acts like a signal that tells your bone marrow to work faster and produce more white blood cells called granulocytes and macrophages. These extra white blood cells help protect your body from bacteria, fungi, and other germs.
common_side_effects: Fever, bone or muscle aches, redness or soreness at the injection site, nausea, diarrhea, rash, and feeling tired are the most common side effects. Some people experience fluid retention, which can cause swelling or puffy ankles.
warnings: Tell your doctor right away if you have chest pain, trouble breathing, rapid heartbeat, or sudden swelling, as these could be signs of a serious reaction. Let your doctor know if you have heart, lung, or kidney problems before starting this medication. It should not be used within 24 hours before or after chemotherapy or radiation therapy. If you have certain types of leukemia or cancers affecting the bone marrow, this medication may not be right for you.
typical_dosing: Sargramostim is given as an injection under the skin or into a vein, usually once a day. The dose and how long you take it depends on your condition and your doctor's instructions. It is typically given in a clinic or hospital, but your doctor may teach you how to give it at home if needed.
